newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy sets out on road to constitutional reform.
newsitem.headline: Italy sets out on road to constitutional reform.

text.p: Italy's new parliamentary reform commission could secure vital constitutional change if it can rise above the squabbling that scuppered past attempts to modernise the political system, commentators said on Thursday.
Parliament on Wednesday night gave final approval to a drive to change the outdated constitution and take steps to give Italy stable government and a more efficient legislature.
"The challenge of reforms takes off," was the headline in Turin's La Stampa newspaper.

Italy has had 54 governments since World War Two and three general elections since 1992 in the upheavals that followed the exposure of entrenched political corruption and the collapse of the old governing class.

Rome's La Repubblica newspaper said Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government needed the commission to succeed if it did not want to be remembered as the "latest impotent and tragic element of continuity with the past".

Most commentators were hopeful the reforms would succeed but some noted the apathy of ordinary Italians and that previous, albeit less ambitious, efforts at reform had become bogged down in their early stages.
"Not surprisingly the reaction of many ... has been to shrug their shoulders," said the economic daily Il Sole 24 Ore.
But Il Sole warned that Italians would face an anguished political and economic future if the commission failed.

Italy could no longer tolerate a situation where "governments have the strength of crickets and the life-span of a leaf," Il Sole said. Future governments should have the power to fire "riotous and inept" ministers.

The new commission of 70 members -- 35 from each house -- will have until June 30 to draft a package of proposed reforms. They will have to be approved individually by two-thirds of each house otherwise they must go to a popular referendum.
Most observers believe the entire package of reforms will go to an umbrella referendum, possibly in mid-1998, the 50th anniversary of the existing constitution.

Virtually all political parties agree on the need to give Italy a federal structure, reduce the number of members of parliament and end the duplication that marks the work of the Chamber and the Senate, slowing legislation to a crawl.
The main differences lie in what powers to invest in the government.

The opposition centre-right, lead by former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, insists that the premier should be directly elected by voters. The centre-left wants the prime minister, now appointed by the president, to have a less direct mandate.
Among the proposals the commission will study is the elimination of the remaining 25 percent of proportional representation in parliament.

Opponents say proportional representation gives small parties a disproportionate amount of power and leads to more political instability than a system that is based on a fully first-past-the post system.
Massimo D'Alema, head of the Decmoratic Party of the Left (PDS), largest party in Prodi's coalition, is the leading candidate to become president of the reform commission.
